title: Chemical protection needs a compatibility check
completeCaptionText:
For a chemical task, the glove material must be compatible with the actual chemical and exposure. Nitrile and neoprene are examples of materials, not a guarantee of protection against every product. Check the SDS and glove manufacturer's information with the trainer. Cotton or leather gloves can absorb liquid and hold it against the skin.

Compare an unused fabric gardening glove with a compatible chemical-resistant glove, using clean props only. Explain why appearance and thickness alone cannot establish chemical resistance. Check that the selected equipment is intact and suitable before putting it on.

Depending on the risk assessment, chemical-resistant coveralls or an apron may also be required. Where harmful dust, vapour or mist may be inhaled, a respirator must be selected for the contaminant and task, with the appropriate filter or cartridge and training. Tight-fitting respiratory protection requires a suitable fit test. A picture of a mask, or a dust mask used for the wrong hazard, does not prove protection.

High-visibility clothing helps other workers see you near machinery, but it does not replace separation from moving equipment. Hearing protection, such as suitable earmuffs or earplugs, may be needed near loud engines or machinery. Use the protection and working arrangements specified for the actual site.
